sentences.text: Ctenochasma is a genus of pterosaur belonging to the suborder Pterodactyloidea, a group within the class Reptilia.
Adult members of this genus possessed an elongated snout lined with over 400 long, thin, and closely packed teeth.
A bony crest running along the skull appeared only in adults and was absent in juvenile specimens.
In the species C. porocristata, a crest along the snout is likely linked to growth or sex rather than defining a specific species.
The smallest known species, C. elegans, reached a maximum adult wingspan of just 1.9 meters.
A unique fossil specimen was discovered in France consisting of a partial skull with a complete neurocranium.
The genus was first described by the German paleontologist Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1851.
However, the name was formally published by von Meyer in 1852.
The original description was based on a single lower jaw filled with crowded teeth.
The species C. gracile was later named by Oppel in 1862 based on a fragmentary skull.
The species now known as C. elegans was originally described as Pterodactylus elegans by Wagner but was renamed because it was named before C. gracile.
Another species, C. porocristata, was named by Paul de Buisonjé in 1981.
There are currently seven recorded fossil occurrences of this genus.
The closely packed teeth formed a comb-like basket traditionally thought to be used for filter feeding, though it lacked the pumping mechanism found in related species.
Researchers suggest the tooth profile indicates a spoonbill-like lifestyle for catching small prey.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Ctenochasma may have been nocturnal with activity patterns similar to modern nocturnal seabirds.
Ctenochasma had larger wings than other ctenochasmatoids and may have flown like modern skuas.
Ctenochasma is classified within the family Ctenochasmatidae, subfamily Ctenochasmatinae, as the sister taxon to the tribe Pterodaustrini.
It belongs to the parent group Lophocratia.
Ctenochasma lived during the Late Jurassic period.
This period spans from the Tithonian to the Berriasian, between 149.2 and 137.05 million years ago.
